summary: Multi-Sector Holdings is, in practice, Berkshire Hathaway. Its third-quarter 2026 operating earnings (our sum of the 10-Q segment lines, excluding investment gains) fell 5.8% to $12.7 billion as underwriting profit and short-term interest income dropped, while railroad, utility and manufacturing earnings rose [1]. It holds about $373 billion of cash and Treasury bills and bought back $9.6 billion of stock in the quarter [1]. The shares are up 13.6% this year against 7.8% for the S&P 500 [10], and the Financials sector trades at 15.0x forward earnings [3]. Smaller holding companies are leveraged and valued on net asset value [6][7][8].

watch: Whether Greg Abel keeps raising buybacks ($9.6 billion in Q3, about $2 billion more in early Q4) given the rule that cash and T-bills never fall below $30 billion [1][10].
Short-term rates: the Fed held at 3.75% to 4% on 28 October with two dissents in favor of a hike, while Berkshire's pre-tax interest income fell 13.9% in Q3 on lower rates [11][1].
Whether insurance underwriting profit keeps normalizing: after-tax underwriting earnings fell 42.9% in Q3 even with no significant catastrophe events in the first nine months [1].
PacifiCorp wildfire litigation tied to the 2020 and 2022 fires, which Berkshire still reports as open [1].
Smaller holdcos: Icahn Enterprises' $4.2 billion CVR Energy refinery purchase, Compass Diversified at 4.5x leverage, and Loews' long-term care reserve charge at CNA [7][8][6].

basics.intro: A multi-sector holding company owns controlling stakes in businesses that have little in common, plus a portfolio of investments, and a small head office allocates the capital. Berkshire Hathaway is the prime example: insurance, a railroad, utilities, manufacturers, retailers and a giant stock portfolio under one roof. Money comes from the operating businesses, from insurance float, and from investment gains. GICS puts it here, not in Industrials, because insurance and investing sit at its core. Pure insurers sit in Insurance, asset managers in Capital Markets, and single-theme conglomerates in Industrial Conglomerates.

products.name: Insurance and reinsurance
products.what: Sells cover against losses, collects premiums up front and invests the money until claims are paid. This is the engine that funds the rest of the group.
products.examples: GEICO, Berkshire Hathaway Reinsurance Group, specialty and workers' compensation insurers

products.name: Regulated infrastructure
products.what: Railroads and utilities earn steady, regulated returns on very large asset bases and need heavy, continuous capital spending.
products.examples: BNSF railway, Berkshire Hathaway Energy, Boardwalk Pipelines at Loews

products.name: Manufacturing, service and retail
products.what: Dozens of independent companies making products and selling services, kept largely autonomous. They send surplus cash to the center.
products.examples: Precision Castparts, Lubrizol, Marmon, Clayton Homes, Pilot, McLane

products.name: Marketable investments
products.what: Large positions in listed companies, held for the long term, plus Treasury bills as a liquidity reserve.
products.examples: Apple, Alphabet, American Express, Bank of America, Coca-Cola

products.name: Net asset value holdcos
products.what: Smaller listed holding companies whose value is mostly their stakes in a few subsidiaries or funds, often financed with debt.

terms.meaning: A company whose main assets are shares in other companies. Its own earnings are the dividends and cash that its subsidiaries send up.
The tendency for a mixed group to trade below the sum of its parts, because investors dislike paying for opaque capital allocation. Berkshire is often argued to be an exception.
Premiums collected before claims are paid. It is money the insurer can invest, and it is cheap or free when underwriting is profitable.
Premiums earned minus claims and expenses. A profit means the float costs nothing; a loss means the float is paid for.
Claims plus expenses divided by premiums. Under 100% is an underwriting profit.
Earnings excluding unrealized and realized investment gains and losses. It matters here because US accounting puts stock-price swings straight into net income, which makes net income noisy.
The market value of a holding company's stakes minus its own debt. Holdcos are judged by the premium or discount of their share price to NAV.
Management's own conservative estimate of what the business is worth. Berkshire's buyback rule is tied to it.
Subsidiary managers run their businesses with little head-office interference, which keeps the center small but makes the group depend on its managers.
Accounting for a large minority stake by recording a share of its profit rather than its market value. Berkshire uses it for Kraft Heinz and Occidental.
The decision of where to put cash: acquisitions, buybacks, new investments, debt repayment or simply holding it. For a holding company this is the main product.
Valuing the group by adding up what each part would be worth on its own, including shares of investees' earnings, rather than using reported profit.

drivers.name: Insurance underwriting results
drivers.how: Catastrophes, claims inflation and pricing swing underwriting profit sharply from year to year. Because the insurers also own most of the investment pool, a bad year hits both profit and float growth.

drivers.name: Short-term interest rates
drivers.how: A very large Treasury bill holding earns interest at the going short-term rate. When rates fall, interest income falls almost one for one, with no change in the businesses.

drivers.name: Stock prices
drivers.how: Marked-to-market gains and losses on the equity portfolio flow through net income, so reported profit can move by tens of billions with no operational change, and equity value follows the market.

drivers.name: Subsidiary cycles
drivers.how: Railroad volumes, utility rate cases, building products and industrial demand follow the economy, so group earnings follow it with a lag and some diversification benefit.

drivers.name: Capital allocation
drivers.how: Buybacks, acquisitions and cash retained all change per-share value. Spending when prices are low adds value; sitting on cash costs relative return.

drivers.name: Premium or discount to book or NAV
drivers.how: The share price relative to net assets reflects trust in management and capital allocation. A narrowing discount lifts the shares without any change in earnings.

business: Berkshire's revenue comes from four places: insurance premiums and investment income, sales by manufacturing, service and retail companies, railroad freight, and regulated utility sales. Total 2025 revenue was $371.4 billion, with $199.5 billion of it from sales and service revenues and $88.9 billion from insurance premiums earned [2]. Smaller holdcos earn from subsidiaries, funds or distributions: Loews from insurer CNA, pipelines and hotels [6].

Customers are extremely varied: drivers who buy GEICO policies, shippers using BNSF, households and businesses on utility grids, and industrial buyers of components and chemicals. Berkshire's decentralized model means the customer base is whatever the subsidiaries serve, so no one client matters at group level [2].

Biggest costs are claims and benefits ($57.3 billion of insurance losses in 2025), cost of sales and services ($160.1 billion), and interest on $130.8 billion of debt at the end of Q3 2026, most of it at BHE and BNSF [2][1]. Holdcos also carry head-office costs, which Berkshire keeps small.

Pricing power sits in the subsidiaries: regulated utilities set returns through rate cases, the railroad through contracts and fuel surcharges, insurers through underwriting discipline. At the holding level the 'pricing power' is capital allocation: Berkshire can buy when others cannot. BNSF revenue per car and BHE rate recovery matter at the segment level [1].

The biggest assets are insurance-company investments (cash and T-bills $372.8 billion, equities $335.5 billion at 30 Sep 2026) and $187.7 billion of railroad and utility property. Biggest liabilities are insurance claims and float of about $178.5 billion, plus $130.8 billion of borrowings [1].

A mix. Insurance and the investment pool are asset-light and capital-rich, while BNSF and BHE are heavily capital-intensive: segment capital spending was $16.1 billion in the first nine months of 2026, of which $10.2 billion at BNSF and BHE together [1].
overview: No industry dataset sizes 'multi-sector holdings' as a market. By scale, Berkshire alone had $1.30 trillion of assets at 30 Sep 2026 and $763.6 billion of shareholders' equity [1]. The other listed holdcos are far smaller: for example Loews' book value per share was $90.24 on 202.9 million shares [6].

The main segments in Berkshire are insurance (GEICO, primary and reinsurance), BNSF, Berkshire Hathaway Energy, manufacturing, service and retailing (including McLane and Pilot), and the investment portfolio. Together the manufacturing, service and retailing businesses earned $11.7 billion after tax in the first nine months of 2026, the biggest operating line [1].

The value chain is unusual: a holdco sits above its businesses and takes their cash. Suppliers and customers belong to the subsidiaries, while the holding company's 'suppliers' are capital markets, reinsurers and the sellers of businesses it buys. Recent buys, OxyChem for about $9.4 billion and Taylor Morrison for about $6.8 billion, show the pattern of buying whole operating companies for cash [1].

The model has evolved from a textile mill into insurance-funded investing, then into owning large operating businesses. The current phase is a CEO handover: Greg Abel took over from Warren Buffett and, per Berkshire's 10-K, the buyback authority passed to the CEO in 2025 [2][10]. Berkshire has not paid a cash dividend since 1967 [2].

Berkshire is Omaha-based with about 387,800 employees at end-2025, roughly 80% in the US [2]. Its railroad and utilities are North American, its insurance and manufacturing are global, and it holds yen-denominated debt (¥2,420 billion par), a sign of non-US financing [1]. Loews, Icahn and Compass are US-centered [6][7][8].
competition: Berkshire has no like-for-like rival of its scale; each segment competes with a different set of firms. The listed holding-company peers that investors compare it to are few and much smaller: Loews, Icahn Enterprises and Compass Diversified [6][7][8]. We could not source a count of competitors for the sub-industry, and we have not verified how GICS classifies each of these peers.

Berkshire is the clear leader by any measure. As of 9 Nov 2026 it was the single largest holding in the Financial Select Sector SPDR fund at 13.12%, ahead of JPMorgan at 11.14% [9]. No market share figure applies to the holdco category itself.

The category is concentrated at the top and fragmented below: one mega-cap, then holdcos with equity in the single-digit billions of NAV, such as Icahn Enterprises at $3.5 billion [7]. Within each of Berkshire's segments competition is separate and in some cases fragmented, as in manufacturing and insurance.

Barriers to entry are mostly capital, reputation and a trusted long-term owner brand. Replicating the group's funding source is hard: float of $178.5 billion at a negative cost has accumulated over decades [1]. Sellers also give Berkshire preference because it pays cash and does not break businesses up, which is why it bought Taylor Morrison for cash [1][12].

Economies of scale are real but of a different kind: low head-office cost, a cheap tax-efficient capital base, and the ability to write checks of $6.8 billion to $9.4 billion in cash without financing [1]. Berkshire's effective tax rate was 18.3% in Q3 2026 [1].

The holding company is differentiated, not commoditized: each one owns different businesses and has a different management style. Subsidiary products are a mix: insurance and chemicals are quite commoditized, while railroads and utilities have local monopolies [1].

Bargaining power is with the holdco when it has cash and with sellers when auctions are competitive. Capital is Berkshire's scarcest and strongest input: $372.8 billion of cash and T-bills lets it be a buyer of last resort [1]. Smaller holdcos depend on lenders: Compass Diversified runs at 4.5x leverage and Icahn Enterprises has $4.4 billion of holdco debt [8][7].
drivers: Revenue growth follows subsidiary growth. At Berkshire, nine-month 2026 revenue rose 8.6% to $301.1 billion, led by sales and service revenue (+13.4%) and acquisitions of OxyChem and Taylor Morrison [1]. For net asset value holdcos, growth is mostly price appreciation of stakes.

Operating margin depends on the mix. Our calculation from the 10-Q: revenue less costs and expenses was 14.5% of revenue in the first nine months of 2026, before investment gains and equity-method earnings, down from 14.6% a year earlier [1]. Insurance underwriting and interest income swing it most.

Key cost variables are insurance claims (catastrophes and inflation), fuel and labor at BNSF, fuel, purchased power and wildfire liabilities at BHE, and raw materials in manufacturing [1]. BNSF earnings rose 19.3% in Q3 2026 despite higher fuel costs [1].

Interest rates matter in both directions. Lower short-term rates cut Berkshire's pre-tax interest and investment income by 13.9% in Q3 2026 [1]. Higher rates raise the cost of debt at BHE and BNSF and weigh on leveraged holdcos like Icahn and Compass [7][8]. The Fed held at 3.75% to 4% on 28 Oct 2026 [11].

GDP and unemployment drive railroad volumes, building products, retail and industrial sales, and so group earnings; inflation drives claims costs and pricing. Oil and refining prices matter for CVR Energy, which is $3.6 billion of Icahn's NAV [7]. Berkshire's holdings in banks and consumer companies are also tied to the economy [1].

Mixed. Insurance float and regulated infrastructure are defensive; manufacturing, retail, rail freight and the equity portfolio are cyclical; and per-share compounding through buybacks and acquisitions is a secular, management-driven growth leg. Third-quarter operating earnings were down 5.8% while the nine-month total rose 8.0%, our calculation from the 10-Q [1].
financials: Revenue growth for Berkshire was 8.6% in the first nine months of 2026 [1], but operating earnings (our sum of segment lines) grew 8.0% to $37.0 billion, versus $34.3 billion in 2025 [1]. Net earnings were $57.9 billion, up from $47.8 billion, helped by $26.4 billion of pre-tax investment gains [1].

Damodaran's January 2026 US dataset has no multi-sector holdings row. The closest proxy, 'Financial Svcs. (Non-bank & Insurance)', shows a 22.19% net margin and 18.48% unadjusted pre-tax operating margin across 176 firms, versus 12.37% net margin for 'Insurance (General)' [4]. Berkshire's own 14.5% pre-investment-gains margin is our calculation from the 10-Q [1].

ROE is lowered by the enormous cash balance. Our estimate: nine-month operating earnings of $37.0 billion annualized over average equity of about $742 billion gives roughly 6.7%; including investment gains the figure is much higher but volatile [1]. ROIC was not available from a source for the category.

Debt is moderate for the group and very uneven by segment. Berkshire reported $45.8 billion of borrowings in insurance and other, against $372.8 billion of cash and T-bills, and $85.0 billion at railroad, utilities and energy [1]. Leveraged peers differ: Compass is at 4.5x, Icahn Enterprises has $4.4 billion of holdco debt on $3.5 billion of NAV, while Loews has $4.4 billion of parent cash against $1.8 billion of debt [8][7][6].

Free cash flow is large and mostly reinvested or held. We did not find a sourced free-cash-flow figure for the category. At Berkshire, the operating businesses and insurers generate the cash that built the $372.8 billion reserve, and the group has paid no dividend since 1967 [1][2].

Capital expenditure is heavy because of the railroad and utilities: $16.1 billion of segment capital spending in nine months of 2026 against $10.3 billion of depreciation and amortization, our reading of the 10-Q segment table [1]. BHE alone spent $7.5 billion and BNSF $2.7 billion [1].

Damodaran's January 2026 forward P/E is 16.38 for Financial Svcs. (Non-bank & Insurance), 21.51 for General Insurance and 27.66 for the whole US market [5]. Berkshire's September repurchases were at roughly 1.4x book, our calculation from the 10-Q [1]. FactSet's current Financials sector forward P/E is 15.0 [3].
risks: Regulation touches each segment: state insurance regulators, rail and utility regulators, and tax law. Berkshire's effective tax rate was 18.3% in Q3 2026 and it discloses exposure to the OECD minimum tax rules [1]. PacifiCorp faces wildfire litigation and utility regulators decide cost recovery [1].

AI matters indirectly: Berkshire's biggest holdings include Alphabet and Apple [1], and AI-driven changes to underwriting and claims could help or hurt GEICO's cost position. We found no sourced estimate of AI's effect on the holding company model itself.

Demographics matter through the insurance book and utility and rail demand: aging populations lift long-term care and health claims, as shown by CNA's $125 million after-tax long-term care reserve charge in Q3 2026 at Loews [6]. At Berkshire the effect is slower and diversified.

Consumer behavior reaches the group through auto insurance (GEICO), homebuilding (Clayton and Taylor Morrison), and retail and consumer brands in the equity portfolio, where consumer products holdings were $112.5 billion at 30 Sep 2026 [1]. Shifts in driving, housing demand and spending feed through.

The main new-competitor risk is for capital, not customers: private equity, sovereign funds and rival holdcos compete to buy businesses. Berkshire has responded with cash deals such as OxyChem (about $9.4 billion) and Taylor Morrison (about $6.8 billion) [1]. Key-person risk after the Buffett handover is a stated risk factor [2].

Geopolitical risks include tariffs and conflicts, which the 10-Q says could affect operating businesses and investments [1]. Berkshire has yen, euro and sterling debt (¥2,420 billion, €4.85 billion and £1.75 billion par), so currency moves hit reported earnings by hundreds of millions each quarter [1].

Substitutes for the holdco model are index funds and private equity: investors can own the underlying sectors directly. Berkshire's ratio to book of about 1.4x and the shares' relative performance show that investors still pay for its structure [1][10], while smaller holdcos typically trade against NAV [7].

opportunities: Large cash and T-bill reserves of $372.8 billion give Berkshire room to buy businesses or stock if prices fall [1].
Repurchases at about 1.4x book can lift per-share value, and the shares outstanding fell from 1,438,223 to 1,418,900 Class A equivalents in nine months [1].
Railroad and utility earnings are growing: BNSF after-tax earnings rose 13.0% and BHE 10.0% in the first nine months of 2026 [1].
Smaller holdcos have specific upside catalysts, such as Icahn's CVR refinery deal that management says lifts nine-month pro forma EBITDA from about $0.9 billion to $2.0 billion [7].
threats: Falling short-term rates will cut interest income on a Treasury bill book that already produced 13.9% less in Q3 [1].
Insurance underwriting profit may normalize or be hit by a major catastrophe, after a nine-month year with none [1].
Succession and key-person risk after the Buffett-to-Abel handover [2].
Wildfire liabilities at PacifiCorp and refinery hedge losses, like Icahn's $522 million in Q3, show how single exposures can swing results [1][7].
horizon.assessment: Over three to five years we think Berkshire's results hinge on two things it controls only partly: how well it deploys a very large cash pile, and whether insurance underwriting stays profitable. Cash earns less if rates fall, so a steady stream of buybacks and acquisitions at sensible prices is what keeps per-share growth going. The operating subsidiaries look steady, with BNSF, BHE and manufacturing all growing earnings in 2026 [1]. The smaller holdcos are more binary, because leverage and one or two big stakes drive NAV [7][8]. Our read is that the category stays tiny in number of companies and dominated by Berkshire's choices.

paragraphs: Multi-sector holdings track the whole economy through their subsidiaries, so the business cycle is felt through several channels at once. Berkshire's nine-month 2026 revenue rose 8.6% to $301.1 billion, helped by acquisitions, and railroad and manufacturing earnings grew faster than insurance [1].

The interest-rate path is the cleanest macro lever. The Fed held its target at 3.75% to 4% on 28 October 2026, with two members voting for a quarter-point rise and the statement saying inflation remains elevated [11]. Berkshire's pre-tax interest and other investment income fell 12.3% in the first nine months of 2026 as short-term rates came down [1]. With roughly $373 billion in cash and Treasury bills, our read is that Berkshire is more exposed to a rate decline than to a rate rise [1]. Higher rates would, however, raise borrowing costs at BHE and BNSF, which carry $85.0 billion of debt [1]. Currency also matters: Berkshire's yen, euro and sterling debt moved pre-tax earnings by a loss of $459 million in Q3 and a gain of $286 million over nine months [1].

No third-party market-size estimate exists for multi-sector holdings, so we describe demand through the subsidiaries. Berkshire's float grew to about $178.5 billion at 30 Sep 2026, from $176 billion at the end of 2025 and $169 billion at the end of 2023 [1][2]. That is slow, steady growth in the pool that funds investing.

Secular drivers sit underneath each business: freight and utility demand, housing, industrial production and insurance penetration. Industrial products revenue rose 28.8% to $12.2 billion in Q3, helped by the OxyChem acquisition [1]. Demand is moderately cyclical: rail volumes and building products fall in downturns, while utilities and insurance are steadier.

Long-term growth for the category comes from reinvestment rather than from market demand. Berkshire deployed about $9.4 billion into OxyChem and about $6.8 billion into Taylor Morrison in 2026 [1]. Demographics matter mainly for insurance claims and for the long-term care exposure seen at CNA, where a $125 million after-tax reserve charge hit Loews in Q3 [6].

Porter's five forces apply segment by segment, but at holding-company level the sharpest forces are rivalry for acquisitions and the bargaining power of capital providers. Threat of new entrants is low for scale holdcos: Berkshire's funding, $178.5 billion of float costing less than zero, took decades to build [1]. Supplier power is limited because the center sources capital, not goods.

Buyer power varies: sellers of private companies have choices, but Berkshire's cash offers, such as Taylor Morrison at $72.50 a share, are hard to match [12]. Substitutes are index funds and private equity for owning diversified businesses. Rivalry among holdcos is limited by the small number of listed peers and their size gap.

Concentration is extreme. Berkshire is 13.12% of XLF, the largest single holding, ahead of JPMorgan at 11.14% [9]. Peers are small: Icahn Enterprises had indicative NAV of $3.5 billion and Loews had parent cash of $4.4 billion against $1.8 billion of debt [7][6]. Compass Diversified is eight consolidated subsidiaries and leverage of 4.5x [8]. Moats are capital, reputation and low-cost float; the weakest point is dependence on a few people.

Political and legal factors reach holding companies via their regulated subsidiaries. PacifiCorp, a BHE utility, faces wildfire litigation from the 2020 fires and the 2022 McKinney Fire, and Berkshire discloses it in each filing [1]. Tax is another: Berkshire's effective rate was 18.3% in Q3 and the 10-Q discusses the OECD Pillar Two minimum tax rules [1].

Economic and trade policy matter. Berkshire's 10-Q warns that wars, trade policies and tariffs could affect operating results and investments, and that investment gains and losses create large volatility in net earnings [1]. Capital-markets regulation applies mostly to listed peers; Compass disclosed material weaknesses in internal controls as of September 2026, which is a reporting risk investors watch [8].

Technological change is mostly indirect: AI and autonomous driving could change auto insurance and claims, and the investment book holds Alphabet and Apple among its five largest positions [1]. Environmental factors include wildfire and catastrophe risk, though Berkshire recorded no significant catastrophe events in the first nine months of 2026 [1]. Governance is a live issue: the 10-K names key-person risk and describes the succession to Greg Abel [2].

Group economics are the sum of very different margin structures. Our calculation from the 10-Q puts revenue less costs and expenses at 14.5% of nine-month 2026 revenue, before investment gains [1]. Damodaran's January 2026 US dataset shows a 22.19% net margin for Non-bank and Insurance financial services, but has no multi-sector holdings row, so this is a loose proxy only [4].

Operating leverage is low at the group level because the businesses are diversified. Insurance after-tax underwriting earnings fell 42.9% in Q3 to $1.35 billion, but a 11.8% rise in manufacturing, service and retailing earnings to $4.04 billion and 19.3% at BNSF cushioned the total [1]. Capital intensity is high in rail and utilities: $16.1 billion of segment capital spending in nine months [1].

Returns on equity are held down by idle cash. Our estimate is about 6.7% on operating earnings, annualized over average equity of about $742 billion [1]. Free cash flow is large but we did not find a sourced figure; the stock of cash and Treasuries stood at $372.8 billion [1]. For smaller holdcos the economics are NAV driven: Icahn Enterprises reported a $225 million Q3 net loss while NAV rose $865 million to $3.47 billion [7].

Berkshire's third-quarter operating earnings, our sum of the 10-Q lines excluding investment gains, were $12.7 billion against $13.5 billion a year earlier, a decline of 5.8%; nine-month operating earnings rose 8.0% to $37.0 billion [1]. Net earnings were $22.1 billion in the quarter against $30.8 billion, because investment gains were smaller [1].

We could not source consensus estimates or revision trends for the category, and Berkshire gives no earnings guidance, so we cannot say where we differ from consensus. For context, FactSet shows Financials as a sector with blended Q3 earnings growth of 6.4% and revenue growth of 6.8%, and the S&P 500 is expected to grow earnings 16.1% in calendar 2027 [3]. Those are sector and index numbers, not holdco estimates.

Our read of the run-rate: insurance underwriting is normalizing from very high levels, and falling short-term rates are a headwind, with after-tax investment income down $447 million in Q3 [1]. Offsetting this are growing railroad, utility and manufacturing earnings and a lower share count from repurchases [1]. Smaller peers are lumpy: Loews' Q3 net income fell to $306 million from $504 million on the CNA reserve charge, and Compass guided 2026 subsidiary adjusted EBITDA to $330 million to $355 million [6][8].

No sector data series exists for multi-sector holdings alone, so we use proxies. FactSet puts the S&P 500 forward P/E at 17.7 and Financials at 15.0, the second lowest of 11 sectors, against a 5-year S&P average of 19.8 [3]. Damodaran's January 2026 forward P/E for Non-bank and Insurance financial services is 16.38, for the total US market 27.66 [5].

Book value is the more useful anchor for a holdco. Our calculation: Berkshire's September repurchases were at an average Class B price of $506.64, about 1.4 times book value of roughly $359 a share [1]. Loews' book value per share was $90.24 at 30 Sep 2026, or $100.67 excluding accumulated other comprehensive income [6]. We did not find a sourced free cash flow yield.

For Berkshire, a modest premium to book implies the market is paying for the cash pile's optionality and for the cash-generating subsidiaries but not a rich growth rate. With the shares up 13.6% this year against 7.8% for the S&P 500, we think the stock no longer looks cheap against its own recent range, though that judgment rests on the book ratio only [10][1]. Icahn Enterprises' price must be read against NAV, and its NAV rests heavily on one position, CVR Energy at $3.6 billion [7].

Berkshire Class B was up 13.6% year to date at 7 November 2026 against 7.8% for the S&P 500, and has risen about 14% since 1 October while the index fell about 4%, a classic defensive rotation [10]. Financials as a group were up 9.66% year to date in XLF at 31 October [9].

Fund ownership is heavy: Berkshire is 13.12% of XLF, which had net assets of $53.6 billion on 9 November, and the fund holds 76 names [9]. Institutional flow and short-interest data for the category were not available from sources we opened, so we do not comment on them.

The largest flow is Berkshire's own: it repurchased $9.6 billion of its stock in Q3, more than twice the Q2 pace per Fortune, and about $2 billion in the first four weeks of Q4 [10]. In its equity book it was a net seller of about $0.4 billion in Q3, trimming banks, insurance and finance by $0.4 billion at cost and adding $2.3 billion in commercial, industrial and other [10]. Breadth within the category is narrow because Berkshire dominates it; the smaller holdcos have thin trading and distribution policies, such as Icahn's $0.50 per unit distribution, that matter more to holders [7].
